items.stem: Which list correctly describes what our solar system contains?

options.text: One star, the eight planets, the dwarf planets and the planets' moons
One star and the eight planets that orbit around it, nothing else
One star, nine planets including Pluto, and the moons of those
Eight planets and their moons, with the Sun counted as a planet

items.why: This is exactly the membership the specification gives: one star, the Sun, the eight planets, the dwarf planets, and the natural satellites that orbit planets.

items.stem: What is meant by a natural satellite?

options.text: A small rocky body that orbits the Sun directly, between the planets
A dwarf planet, which orbits the Sun beyond the eight planets
A moon: a body that orbits a planet rather than orbiting the Sun
A man-made craft kept in orbit by its engines, not gravity

items.why: The specification defines natural satellites as the moons that orbit planets, and states that they are part of the solar system.

items.stem: Which statement describes how our solar system relates to the Milky Way?

options.text: The Milky Way is just another name for our own solar system
Our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy
The Milky Way galaxy holds everything in the universe
Our solar system lies at the exact centre of the Milky Way

items.why: The specification states directly that our solar system is a small part of the Milky Way galaxy.

items.stem: How was the Sun formed?

options.text: From a cloud of dust and gas squeezed together by magnetism
From a huge ball of chemical fuel that was set alight in space
From a cloud of dust and gas in which fusion started at once
From a cloud of dust and gas pulled together by gravity

items.why: The specification states that the Sun was formed from a cloud of dust and gas (nebula) pulled together by gravitational attraction.

items.stem: What determines the life cycle that a star will follow?

options.text: The colour of the star, which shows its surface state
How bright the star looks when viewed from Earth
The size of the star, which sets the path it takes
The age of the star, since all stars follow one path

items.why: The specification states that the life cycle of a star is determined by the size of the star.

items.stem: A star about the size of the Sun leaves the main sequence. What happens next?

options.text: It explodes straight away as a supernova
It shrinks back to become a protostar
It becomes a white dwarf at once
It expands and becomes a red giant

items.why: For a star of about the Sun's size, the stage after the main sequence is the red giant.

items.stem: What is the full sequence of stages at the end of the life of a star about the size of the Sun?

options.text: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf
Red giant, then supernova, then a neutron star
Red super giant, then supernova, then black hole
White dwarf, then red giant, then a black dwarf

items.why: A star of about the Sun's size swells into a red giant, collapses to a white dwarf, and finally cools to a black dwarf.

items.stem: What happens to a star much more massive than the Sun after the main sequence?

options.text: Red giant, then white dwarf, then black dwarf, just as the Sun will
Red super giant, then supernova, then neutron star or black hole
Red super giant, then supernova, then always a black hole
Red super giant, then protostar, then a new main sequence star

items.why: A star much more massive than the Sun becomes a red super giant, explodes as a supernova, and leaves a neutron star or a black hole.

items.stem: What can be left at the centre after a massive star explodes as a supernova?

options.text: A black hole, whatever the mass of the star that exploded
A white dwarf that later cools to become a black dwarf
A neutron star, or a black hole if the star was massive enough
Nothing at all, as the star is completely destroyed

items.why: A supernova leaves a very dense neutron star, and for the most massive stars a black hole.

items.stem: Which elements are produced by fusion processes in stars?

options.text: Only hydrogen and helium, and nothing more
Only those elements that are heavier than iron
All of the naturally occurring elements
Only elements made by the splitting of nuclei

items.why: The specification states that fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements.

items.stem: Where are the elements heavier than iron produced?

options.text: In the explosion of a massive star, a supernova
In the fusion reactions inside a main sequence star
Nowhere; they have existed from the very start
By the splitting of very large nuclei inside the star

items.why: The specification states that elements heavier than iron are produced in a supernova.

items.stem: What allows a planet or a satellite to maintain a circular orbit?

options.text: Gravity provides the force that keeps it in its circular orbit
There is no gravity in space, so it just keeps drifting round
Its engines fire all the time to hold it in its orbital path
An outward force balances gravity and holds it in place

items.why: The specification states that gravity provides the force that allows planets and satellites, both natural and artificial, to maintain their circular orbits.

items.stem: At the start of a star's life cycle, why do fusion reactions begin?

options.text: Gravity draws the dust and gas together, heating it until nuclei fuse
The dust and gas catch fire and burn chemically, giving out the energy
Fusion starts as soon as gravity begins to draw the cloud inwards
Magnetic forces squeeze the cloud until its particles join together

items.why: Gravitational attraction pulls the material of the nebula together; the compression raises the temperature and density until fusion reactions start.

items.stem: Which two effects are in equilibrium in a stable star?

options.text: No effects at all, because equilibrium means no forces act on it
The inward pull of gravity and the outward push of gravity itself
The weight of the star and the upthrust of the gas around it
The gravitational collapse inwards and the expansion due to fusion energy

items.why: The specification states that fusion reactions lead to an equilibrium between the gravitational collapse of a star and its expansion due to fusion energy.

items.stem: A main sequence star stays the same size for billions of years. Why?

options.text: No forces act inside a star once it reaches the main sequence
Its inward collapse and its outward expansion stay balanced
Gravity pushes the star outwards as hard as it pulls it inwards
The upthrust of the gas around it supports the star's weight

items.why: While fusion continues at a steady rate, the expansion due to fusion energy exactly balances the gravitational collapse, so the star's size does not change.

items.stem: What does the explosion of a massive star do to the elements it has produced?

options.text: It leaves the elements locked inside the remnant star
It distributes the elements throughout the whole universe
It destroys the elements, leaving only hydrogen gas
It converts all the elements into ones lighter than iron

items.why: The specification states that the explosion of a massive star (supernova) distributes the elements throughout the universe.

items.stem: How do fusion processes in stars lead to the formation of new elements?

options.text: Large nuclei split apart to form smaller nuclei of new elements
Atoms join chemically to make new compounds and elements
Fusion makes only the elements heavier than iron in the core
Small nuclei join to form larger nuclei of different elements

items.why: In fusion, small nuclei join to form a larger nucleus. Because the number of protons changes, the new nucleus is a nucleus of a different element.

items.stem: Which statement correctly compares moons and artificial satellites?

options.text: Both orbit a planet, but only the moon is held there by gravity
Both orbit a planet; moons are natural and satellites are man-made
Both orbit the Sun directly, and both were formed with the Sun
Neither one is held by gravity, since gravity does not act in space

items.why: Moons and artificial satellites both orbit a planet and are both held in orbit by gravity. The distinction is that moons are natural and satellites are made by people.

items.stem: (HT only) A satellite travels round a circular orbit at a steady rate. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Its speed and its velocity are both remaining constant
Its speed keeps increasing because gravity acts upon it
Its speed stays the same but its velocity is changing
Its velocity is constant but its speed is changing

items.why: In a circular orbit gravity acts at right angles to the motion, so it changes the direction of travel and therefore the velocity, while the speed is unchanged.

items.stem: (HT only) A satellite in a stable circular orbit is made to travel faster. For the orbit to stay stable, what must happen?

options.text: The radius of the orbit must become much larger
The radius of the orbit can stay exactly as before
The orbit turns into a straight line at once
The radius of the orbit must get smaller

items.why: For a stable orbit the radius must change if the speed changes: a faster orbital speed corresponds to a smaller orbital radius.

items.stem: Light from a distant galaxy is compared with light from the same element produced in a laboratory on Earth. What is observed about the light from the galaxy?

options.text: Its wavelength is longer than the laboratory value
Its wavelength is shorter than the value on Earth
It looks red instead of its normal colour
It has been reddened by dust on the way here

items.why: Red-shift is an observed increase in the wavelength of light from most distant galaxies, so the galaxy's light arrives with a longer wavelength than the same light produced on Earth.

items.stem: The light from most distant galaxies shows red-shift. What does this observation provide evidence for?

options.text: That the galaxies fly out through existing space
That the Earth sits at the centre of the universe
That space itself, the universe, is expanding
That the distant galaxies are slowing down

items.why: The specification states that the observed red-shift provides evidence that space itself (the universe) is expanding.

items.stem: According to the Big Bang theory, what was the universe like at the very beginning?

options.text: A giant star that collapsed and then blew apart
A single giant star that exploded out into space
A large empty space that matter exploded into
A very small region, extremely hot and dense

items.why: The specification states that the Big Bang theory suggests the universe began from a very small region that was extremely hot and dense.

items.stem: What do observations of supernovae made since 1998 onwards suggest about distant galaxies?

options.text: They are gradually slowing as they recede
They are receding ever faster as time goes on
They will slow to a stop and then fall back
The nearest of them are receding fastest

items.why: The specification states that since 1998 onwards, observations of supernovae suggest that distant galaxies are receding ever faster.

items.stem: Which statement about dark mass and dark energy matches what the specification says?

options.text: They are fully explained by the Big Bang theory
They both name the same invisible material
They are examples of what is still not understood
The 1998 supernova results predicted them both

items.why: The specification states that there is still much about the universe that is not understood, for example dark mass and dark energy.

items.stem: Every distant galaxy is observed to be receding, and the further away a galaxy is the faster it recedes. Why is this evidence that the universe is expanding?

options.text: Because the galaxies were thrown outwards through space
Because the Earth must be at the centre of it all
Because space between all the galaxies is stretching
Because nearer galaxies are moving away faster

items.why: The change of each galaxy's speed with distance is what the specification names as evidence of an expanding universe: space itself grows, so more distant galaxies separate from us faster.

items.stem: How does the observed red-shift provide evidence for the Big Bang model?

options.text: The stretched light is left over from the original explosion
It proves the Big Bang, so the theory can never be changed
The red colour shows the early universe was very hot
An expanding universe must once have been small and dense

items.why: Red-shift shows the universe is expanding; running that expansion backwards leads to the very small, extremely hot and dense beginning the Big Bang theory suggests.

items.stem: Which statement best describes how scientists were able to use observations to arrive at the Big Bang theory?

options.text: A model was proposed to explain what was observed
Red-shift observations proved the theory to be true
Nobody saw the beginning, so the theory is untestable
The theory came from the 1998 supernova observations

items.why: Scientists build a theory that accounts for the observations, such as red-shift, and keep testing that theory against further observations.

items.stem: Observations of supernovae made since 1998 onwards changed what scientists say about the expansion of the universe. What does this show about scientific theories?

options.text: A theory becomes a fact once the evidence supports it
New observations can change an accepted theory
Theories about the distant past can never be tested
The older theory must have been an untested idea

items.why: Scientists use observations to arrive at theories, and a theory such as the Big Bang is developed further when new evidence, such as the supernova observations, arrives.

items.stem: The light from galaxy B shows a bigger observed increase in wavelength than the light from galaxy A. What can be concluded about galaxy B?

options.text: It is moving faster, so it must be closer to us
It is further away than A and is moving faster
It is nearer than A and is moving more slowly
It is a larger and brighter galaxy than A

items.why: The specification states that the further away the galaxies, the faster they are moving and the bigger the observed increase in wavelength.

items.stem: The pattern of lines in the spectrum of a distant galaxy is compared with the pattern produced by the same element on Earth. What is observed?

options.text: The lines are shifted towards the blue end
The whole galaxy appears red rather than white
The lines are brighter and further apart
The lines are all shifted towards the red end

items.why: Red-shift is seen as the whole pattern of lines from a known element appearing at longer wavelengths than the laboratory pattern.

items.stem: Light from galaxies X, Y and Z is examined. X shows a small increase in wavelength, Y a medium increase and Z a large increase. Which galaxy is furthest away?

options.text: Z, because it shows the biggest increase
X, because it shows the smallest increase
Y, because its shift shows a medium-sized galaxy
X, because it has lost the most speed

items.why: The bigger the observed increase in wavelength, the faster the galaxy is moving and the further away it is, so Z is the most distant of the three.
